diagnostic_evidence.quote: to obtain unique identification of drift terms in  the additive noise, it suffices to let  $\mathcal Q=\{\xi\in \mathbb Z^d: \mathbb E \widehat u_0(\xi)\neq 0\}$ satisfy the condition in Proposition \ref{prop-drift-identification}
We only show the proof in the multiplicative noise case since that in additive noise case is similar.

issues.failure_explanation:
The proposition covers both noise cases (its proof treats the additive case as 'similar'), but its hypothesis only requires $\widehat u_0(\xi)
eq 0$ a.s. The additive-case proof (Appendix sec3-appendix-prop1) identifies the drift from $\mathbb E\widehat u(t_2,\xi)/\mathbb E\widehat u(t_1,\xi)$, which is valid only when $\mathbb E\widehat u_0(\xi)
eq 0$. Under the stated hypothesis this ratio can be 0/0 (e.g., random $u_0$ whose Fourier coefficients are a.s. nonzero but mean zero, so all averaged modes vanish and the averaged snapshots carry no drift information), making the proof's division invalid and the conclusion unsupported in the additive case. The paper's own appendix states the needed hypothesis is $\mathcal Q=\{\xi:\mathbb E\widehat u_0(\xi)
eq 0\}$, contradicting the proposition as stated.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restate the proposition with case-specific hypotheses: in the additive case require $\mathcal Q=\{\xi:\mathbb E\widehat u_0(\xi)\neq 0\}$ (exactly the condition the appendix already uses); the multiplicative case is unchanged.
issues.overall_effect: The additive-noise case of the drift-identifiability guarantee in Proposition prop-drift-identification is unsupported as stated for random initial data; any reliance on the proposition in the additive case inherits the gap.
issues.title: Additive-noise case of drift identifiability proposition uses an insufficient Fourier-mode hypothesis
issues.why_classification: A local hypothesis correction, already supplied by the paper's own appendix; all substantive conclusions survive once the correct condition is stated.

issues.failure_explanation: In the multiplicative case $\widehat u(t_2,\xi)/\widehat u(t_1,\xi)=e^{c_1\Delta t}e^{c_2(W(t_2)-W(t_1))}$, so its lifted phase is $\Im(c_1)\Delta t+\Im(c_2)(W(t_2)-W(t_1))$. The Brownian increment is an unbounded Gaussian, so for every $\Delta t>0$ there is positive probability that the principal argument differs from the lifted phase by a nonzero multiple of $2\pi$. Hence $\mathbb E[\operatorname{Arg}(\cdot)]\neq\Im(c_1)\Delta t$ exactly, identity (dri-mul-ide2) fails, and the claim that small $|t_2-t_1|$ removes the ambiguity is false. The linear system for the odd-order drift coefficients is contaminated by $2\pi$-multiples (different per mode), so the exact uniqueness conclusion for the odd coefficients is unproven. The pathwise analogue prop:added-2 is derived from the same equations (mul-ide-1)-(mul-ide-2).

failure_location.quote: Notice that for $|t_2-t_1|>0$ sufficiently small, the phase ambiguity in \eqref{mul-ide-2} can be removed.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the statistic with a wrap-free one, e.g. identify the odd coefficients from the argument of $\mathbb E[(\widehat u(t_2,\xi)/\widehat u(t_1,\xi))/|\widehat u(t_2,\xi)/\widehat u(t_1,\xi)|]$ (whose phase equals $\Im(c_1)\Delta t$ exactly for small $\Delta t$, since the radial factor is real positive), and rerun the same full-rank linear argument; for prop:added-2 condition on the no-wrap event or accept an explicit error term.
issues.overall_effect: Exact identifiability of the odd-order drift coefficients in the multiplicative case (Proposition prop-drift-identification) and the pathwise result prop:added-2 are unproven as stated.
issues.title: Phase-wrap gap invalidates the odd-coefficient identification in the multiplicative drift result
issues.why_classification: The stated conclusion (exact a.s. identifiability) survives, but the repair requires replacing the identification statistic and rederiving the expectation identities: a contained nontrivial argument rather than a routine local edit.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: $$V_1=\text{span} \Big\{\sum_{k=1}^{M_{\epsilon}}c_k(-1)^l\frac {(\lambda_kt-\mu t)^l}{l!}e^{q_k W(t)}\phi_k(x), l=0,1\cdots,L_{\epsilon}\Big\}.$$
$V_4=\text{span} \Big\{\sum_{k=1}^{M'}(-1)^l\int_0^t \frac {((\lambda_k-\mu)(t-s))^l}{l!}q_k R_k dW(s) \phi_k(x), l=0,1\cdots,L_{\epsilon}\Big\}.$
\|u(t)-P_{V}u(t)\|_{L^2(\Omega;H)}\lesssim  \epsilon (1+\|u_0\|_{L^2(\Omega;H)})\;.

issues.failure_explanation: Read literally (an existentially quantified $V$ for each $t$), the statement is vacuous: $V=\mathrm{span}\{u(t)\}$ has dimension 1 and zero error. The proof indeed constructs only spaces depending on $t$ and on the noise realization ($V_1$ contains random vectors built from $e^{q_kW(t)}$; the additive-case $V_4$ is spanned by stochastic integrals $\int_0^t(\cdot)\,dW(s)$), so no fixed/deterministic space is produced, despite $P_V$ being applied to $u(t)$ in $L^2(\Omega;H)$. Under the meaningful deterministic reading (the 'data space' interpretation advertised in the introduction), the logarithmic dimension is false under the stated hypotheses: in the additive case the stochastic convolution $\int_0^te^{\mathcal L(t-s)}\mathcal G R\,dW(s)$ has a covariance operator whose nonzero spectrum coincides with that of the time-kernel operator with kernel $\langle e^{\mathcal Ls}\mathcal GR,e^{\mathcal Ls'}\mathcal GR\rangle$; with only power-law decay of $|q_kR_k|^2$ (admissible under the summability hypothesis) this kernel has finitely many derivatives, so the covariance eigenvalues and hence the optimal deterministic $d$-dimensional approximation error decay only polynomially, requiring $d$ polynomial in $1/\epsilon$. In the multiplicative case at $t=0$, the allowed random initial data (only $|c_k|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le\theta k^{-\gamma}$ assumed) likewise forces polynomial dimension. Thus the advertised $O(|\log\epsilon|^2)$-dimensional strong-sense parabolic data space is neither established nor true.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: K(x,y)=\int_0^T \mathbb E \left[u(s,x)u(s,y)\right]ds,\;G(s,t)=\int_{\mathcal D} \mathbb E \left[u(t,x)u(s,x)\right]dx,
Thus, by the chain rule, $G(s,t)=\int_{\mathcal D} \mathbb E u(t,x)u(s,x)dx=\int_{\mathcal D} \mathbb E u(t, X_{t,0}(x))u(s, X_{s,0}(x))dx$ is differentiable with respect to $x$.
The differentiability of $G(s,t)$, i.e., $G(s,t)\in \mathcal C^{p}([0,T]^2)$ leads to $\lambda_j= o(j^{-(p+1)})$ (see, e.g., \cite{MR728689}).
Notice that the eigenvalues of $K$ and $G$ are non-negative satisfying $\lambda_1\ge \lambda_2\ge \cdots\ge \lambda_j\ge \cdots$ with $\lambda_j\to 0$ as $j\to \infty.$

issues.failure_explanation: The proof asserts that the space covariance $K$ (an operator on $H$) and the time covariance $G$ (an operator on $L^2([0,T])$) share one eigenvalue sequence and that both projection errors equal the same tail sum. Pathwise the corresponding operators are $A_\omega A_\omega^*$ and $A_\omega^*A_\omega$ and share spectra, but $K=\mathbb E[A_\omega A_\omega^*]$ and $G=\mathbb E[A_\omega^*A_\omega]$ are expectations, and averaged operators need not share spectra (e.g., a two-mode field $f_1g_1\xi_1+f_2g_2\xi_2$ with correlated amplitudes yields rank-one $K$ but rank-two $G$). Moreover, the displayed identity for $G(s,t)$ is not a valid change of variables (no Jacobian, mismatched flows), and spatial ($x$-) differentiability of the stochastic flow is used to conclude $G\in C^p([0,T]^2)$, i.e., smoothness in the time variables, which the Brownian-driven flow does not possess pathwise. Hence the decay $\lambda_j=o(j^{-(p+1)})$ is not established for the operator actually used, and the time-side projections $P_{V_G^k}$ do not even produce a finite-dimensional subspace of $L^2([0,T];H)$. The claimed $o(\epsilon^{-2/p})$-dimensional space-time approximation is therefore unproven.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Rebuild the proof on the space-side kernel: $K(x,y)=\int_0^T\mathbb E[u_0(X_{t,0}(x))u_0(X_{t,0}(y))]dt$ is genuinely $C^p(\mathcal D\times\mathcal D)$ by the $C^p$ spatial regularity of the flow, so $\int_0^T\mathbb E\|u(t)-P_{V_K^k}u(t)\|^2dt$ equals the tail of $K$'s eigenvalues; cite the correct eigenvalue decay for $C^p$ kernels on $d$-dimensional domains, adjust the dimension exponent accordingly, and drop the false shared-spectrum chain and the $G$-smoothness argument.
issues.overall_effect: Lemma lem:added-1 (hyperbolic data-space dimension) and the hyperbolic versus parabolic comparisons built on it in the introduction and conclusion are unsupported as stated.
issues.title: Hyperbolic data-space lemma: false spectrum identification and flawed kernel-smoothness argument
issues.why_classification: A comparable polynomial-dimension hyperbolic data-space result appears recoverable with contained work via the space-side kernel, but the proof's chain of equalities must be rebuilt and the stated dimension exponent changes, so the repair is more than local yet avoids major loss.

issues.failure_explanation: First, the proof is invalid for the random initial data the proposition allows: $w_\epsilon$ is built from the random coefficients $c_k$, while the target $\mathbb E[u_{M_\epsilon}(t)]=\sum_k\mathbb E[c_k]e^{i\lambda_kt}e^{-q_k^2t/2}\phi_k$ is deterministic; the difference contains the irreducible fluctuation $\sum_k(\mathbb E[c_k]-c_k)(\cdot)$, which the Taylor-tail bound does not control (for mean-zero $c_k$ the claimed inequality fails at $O(1)$ level). The chain then silently replaces $\mathbb E[u_{M_\epsilon}(t)]$ by $u_{M_\epsilon}(t)$ in (nls-est2), comparing the solution with its damped mean, an $O(1)$ discrepancy presented as $O(\epsilon)$. Second, the statement is per-time existential and hence vacuous ($V=\mathrm{span}\{\mathbb Eu(t)\}$ gives zero error with dimension 1), while the intended trajectory-level claim advertised in the introduction is false in general: $\mathbb Eu(t)=\sum_k\bar c_ke^{i\lambda_kt}e^{-q_k^2t/2}\phi_k$ undergoes unitary oscillation (e.g. $\mathcal G=\mathrm{Id}$, $q_k\equiv1$, which satisfies all stated hypotheses including admissibility of $\mathcal G^*\mathcal G=I$), and on any interval where incommensurate modes with amplitudes above $\epsilon$ are active the Kolmogorov width of the averaged trajectory is polynomial in $1/\epsilon$.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: The algorithm terminates when the  regression error does not improve.
the initial guesses for the non-zero  entries are fixed at $10$

issues.failure_explanation: The only termination check breaks when the residual strictly increases. If a support repeats ($\mathcal I^{\ell+1}=\mathcal I^\ell$, possible when Step 2 retains the old support), Step 3 solves the identical nonlinear regression and, with the deterministic solver (initial guesses fixed at 10), returns the same point; the residual is then unchanged, the else-branch continues, and the algorithm repeats the same state forever. Additionally, breaking at $\ell=0$ sets $\widehat{\bc}^{*}=\widehat{\bc}^{(0)}$, which is never defined, and outputs $\mathcal I^{*}=\emptyset$, violating the stated output contract $|\mathcal I^{*}|=j$. The prose states the intended non-strict test ('terminates when the regression error does not improve'), which the pseudocode does not implement.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Change the termination test to break when the residual does not strictly improve (matching the prose), initialize $\widehat{\bc}^{(0)}$ or handle the $\ell=0$ break by returning the first-iteration result, and optionally add an iteration cap; apply the same correction to the SP pseudocode.
issues.overall_effect: Algorithm QSPalgo is not guaranteed to terminate or to return a defined $j$-sparse output as specified; the transcribed SP pseudocode shares the same break-logic defect.
issues.title: QSP termination condition can loop forever and references an undefined iterate
issues.why_classification: A one-line logic fix matching the stated prose; no mathematical content or advertised behavior is lost.

which is a standard normal variable with  cumulative distribution function (CDF) $\Phi$ under the null hypothesis.
Then for some significance level $p^* \in (0,1)$

issues.failure_explanation: Under the null $Z_N\sim N(0,1)$, so a level-$p^*$ test must compare $|Z_N|$ with an upper quantile such as $\Phi^{-1}(1-p^*/2)$. As written, for any standard significance level $p^*<1/2$ one has $\Phi^{-1}(p^*)<0$, so $2|Z_N|\ge\Phi^{-1}(p^*)$ always holds (the rule always declares multiplicative noise) and the additive branch $2|Z_N|<\Phi^{-1}(p^*)/2$ is never satisfied. Even for $p^*>1/2$ the two thresholds leave an undecided region with no specified action. The claimed false-positive-rate control therefore does not follow from the stated decision rule.

failure_location.quote: we decide that the diffusion part contains multiplicative noise if $2|Z_N|\geq \Phi^{-1}(p^*)$, and it is only additive if $2|Z_N|<\Phi^{-1}(p^*)/2$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the thresholds with a valid two-sided test, e.g., decide multiplicative if $|Z_N|>\Phi^{-1}(1-p^*/2)$ and additive otherwise (removing or explicitly handling the undecided region), and restate the false-positive control accordingly.
issues.overall_effect: The additive-noise detection shortcut of Section 5.2 (skipping the diffusion feature construction) does not implement the claimed statistical test; its decisions are unreliable as specified.
issues.title: Additive-noise detection test has degenerate thresholds and no false-positive control
issues.why_classification: Routine local correction of the decision thresholds; the fallback full diffusion-identification procedure preserves correctness, so only the shortcut's justification is affected.
